Frank Gehry. The Canadian-American architect known for deconstructionist and expressionist buildings that challenge conventional form through billowing titanium surfaces and fragmented geometries.

Gehry was born in 1929. His most famous work is the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, completed in 1997. It's a curved titanium-clad structure that became an international landmark and revitalized the Basque industrial city through architectural tourism. He created the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles in 2003, featuring steel and aluminum sails evoking billowing fabric, and this building redefined the civic concert venue. He also designed the Dancing House in Prague in 1992, a playfully tilted structure with undulating glass and stone that mimics a pair of dancers.

Gehry pioneered the use of computer modeling with CATIA software to design complex curved forms that would be impossible to build using traditional methods. His Santa Monica residence from 1978 wrapped his own modest house in corrugated metal and plywood, a radical statement about material and beauty. His buildings are known for deconstructed, fragmented exteriors that appear to deconstruct and reassemble form, rejecting the clean lines of modernism.

His work merges fine art sensibilities with architecture. He often collaborates with artists and creates buildings as sculptural objects. This approach connects him to earlier figures like Antoni Gaudí, who also pursued a sculptural, organic vision and rejected rigidity, though Gehry operates through digital complexity. He shares a contemporary pursuit of flowing, curved forms with Zaha Hadid, though they express similar aesthetic visions differently. His architecture embodies the philosophical movement of deconstruction, fragmenting and reassembling conventional building logic.
